title: The ILO's annual conference in Geneva: what happens in June
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Two weeks every June, 187 member States, one agenda on the world of work.
body:
Each June, ministers, employers and trade union leaders from around the world gather in Geneva for the **International Labour Conference (ILC)**, the supreme body of the International Labour Organization. It is often called an international parliament of labour. It sets international labour standards and the broad policies of the ILO, and it is also a forum where the key social and labour questions of the day are discussed. This post explains how the Conference works, what happened at its 2025 session, and why an event in Geneva matters to a worker in an Indian factory or on a construction site.

## The unusual idea behind the ILO

The ILO is unusual among international bodies because it is **tripartite**. Governments, employers and workers all take part, and each has its own vote. Under the ILO Constitution, every member State sends **four representatives** to the Conference: two government delegates, one employers' delegate and one workers' delegate. Each delegate may bring advisers, up to two for each item on the agenda, who speak but cannot vote unless a delegate appoints them as a deputy. The Conference also examines the credentials of delegates, and can refuse a delegate by a two-thirds vote of those present.

The workers' delegate speaks for workers independently of the government delegation, which means that in principle a trade union can disagree with its own government in the open, in front of the world.

## How the Conference works

In the first week or so, delegates sit in committees that handle technical items: a standard-setting committee, for instance, goes through a draft convention paragraph by paragraph, and other committees look at how existing standards are applied. The plenary hears reports and speeches and takes the final votes, including on the ILO's programme and budget.

The key rule concerns standards. Adoption of a **Convention** or a **Recommendation** requires a **two-thirds majority** of the votes cast by delegates present on the final vote. A Convention is open to ratification by member States and becomes legally binding on those that ratify it. A Recommendation carries no ratification and is guidance, often adopted alongside a Convention to give practical detail. After a session, each member State must bring a newly adopted Convention before its competent authorities within one year, or in no case later than 18 months in exceptional circumstances. If those authorities do not agree to ratify, the State's remaining duty is to report periodically on its law and practice.

## The 113th session, June 2025

The 113th session was held in Geneva from 2 to 13 June 2025 and, according to the ILO, drew more than 5,400 delegates representing governments, employers' organisations and workers' organisations. The ILO has 187 member States. During the session, 18 instruments of ratification from eight member States were registered, and seven amendments to the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 were approved by an overwhelming majority.

Two items stood out:

- **Biological hazards.** The Conference adopted the ILO's first international labour standards on preventing exposure to biological hazards at work: Convention No. 192 with an accompanying Recommendation. The Convention requires national occupational safety and health policies to cover biological hazards and emergency preparedness, and requires employers to take preventive measures with workers, who must be informed and trained.
- **Decent work in the platform economy.** The Conference held a first discussion on a possible new standard for platform workers and agreed that the outcome should be a Convention supplemented by a Recommendation. The discussion continues at the 114th session, which the ILO schedules for Geneva from 1 to 12 June 2026, with the aim of adopting both texts. We take up this item in the next post.

## The workers' group and India

Workers' delegates from all countries form the **Workers' Group**, which meets to coordinate positions on each agenda item, in the same way that employers form their own group. For the workers' side, the importance lies in numbers: a united group can press for stronger language in a draft, while a divided group weakens its hand.

BMS has said that it has taken part in the Conference as one of the central trade union organisations of India, and its leaders have addressed committees and the plenary on subjects such as social protection, informality and decent work. For India, where around nine in ten workers are in informal work according to the India Employment Report 2024, the subjects chosen in Geneva are not remote. Platform work, safety at work and social protection are questions that affect Indian workers directly.

## Why it matters to a worker in India

A Convention adopted in Geneva does not change Indian law by itself. India decides whether to ratify it, and it must first bring the text before Parliament or the competent authority within the period mentioned above. Even so, standards adopted by the Conference serve as a reference point. A trade union can point to them when asking for a law or a scheme, a government can draw on them when designing one, and an employer can see what is likely to be expected in the future.

The process also gives workers a seat while a standard is written. Delegates can propose amendments, vote on them, and argue the case for more protection, and that is a very different position from being told about a standard after it has been agreed.

## What to watch

- **The second discussion on platform work in 2026**, and whether the final text is a convention that India can ratify.
- **Ratification of Convention No. 192**, which depends on each country's own decision.
- **The role of workers' representatives from developing countries**, where informality is widespread and where the standards must work for people with no formal employer.

## Closing

The ILC is easy to overlook, since its work runs for two weeks and its outcome is a text. But a text agreed in Geneva in June can shape the laws that ministers pass in the following years. For a trade union, taking part in that process, and bringing the concerns of Indian workers to it, is part of the work.
